title: Describing things
job: Size, colour, quality — agreement at length
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: GERMAN'S AGREEMENT LIVES IN THE ARTICLE, not on the adjective. The grid is der / die / das in the nominative, den / die / das in the accusative, and dem / der / dem in the dative, with ein, eine, einen, einem, einer and the kein series beside them. L1 shipped every one of those words across five modules without ever laying them out; this is where they become a table.

AND HERE IS WHAT THE GRID BUYS: because the case is marked on the article, German word order is FREE in a way English's is not. Den Apfel esse ich is an ordinary sentence meaning "I'm eating the apple", with the object first — den says it is the object, so the position no longer has to. English marks its object by position alone, and this is the deepest structural delta in the course.

Adjectives stay PREDICATIVE throughout this level — Das Auto ist rot — where they take no ending at all. The attributive declension (ein guter Mann, der gute Mann, guter Wein: three declensions chosen by what stands in front) is too large to sit beside a module teaching colours, and it belongs to L3.

GENDER IS A PROPERTY OF THE WORD and is not predictable from meaning. das Mädchen is neuter; der Löffel and die Gabel sit at the same table with different genders. Learn every noun with its article, and refuse the shortcuts — a rule that fails on the first table setting is worse than no rule.
weiß carries an ß and the index KEEPS it, so Maße and Masse are two different keys. Never respell it ss, and never write a display in capitals: a shouted STRASSE folds to a key no row owns.

words.note: After ist it takes no ending, and it never will at this level. In front of a noun it would decline, and that is L3's.
Neuter — das Auto — and its plural simply adds -s, which is unusual in German and comes from the word being borrowed.

sentences.trap: The gender is in das and nowhere else. rot tells you nothing about the car, which is exactly why the article has to be learnt with the noun.
sentences.sound: das OW-toh ist ROHT. The final t of rot is fully sounded.

variations.changed: a masculine noun, so a different article
a feminine noun and a different colour
a different colour

mistake.why: After ist the adjective takes no ending: Das Auto ist rot.

sentences.usage: Naming which one you mean, in a car park or a shop.
sentences.mnemonic: The article carries the gender. The adjective carries nothing.

words.note: The sch is one sound, a sh, and the final z is a ts. Four letters at the front and one sound out of them.
The ß is a long s and the index keeps it — weiss would be a different key entirely. It is also spelled weiss in Switzerland, which this course does not write.

sentences.trap: Tür is feminine and Auto is neuter, and there is nothing about a door or a car that says so. The article is a fact about the word.
sentences.sound: dee TUER ist GRUEN. Both words carry the ü, and it is the same sound in each.

variations.changed: a different colour
a neuter noun and the ß colour
a masculine noun

mistake.why: The ß is never respelled: Das Auto ist weiß.

sentences.mnemonic: ß is a letter and the index knows it.

words.note: sehen changes its vowel for du and for the third person — du siehst, er sieht — as sprechen and geben do.
The g is hard and the b at the end goes to a p sound. German devoices every final b, d and g.

sentences.trap: der becomes den when the noun is the object, and ONLY in the masculine. die, das and the plural die look identical in both cases, which is why the masculine is where the accusative is visible at all.
sentences.sound: ikh ZAY-uh dayn AP-fel. The ch of ich is the front sound, made near the palate.

variations.changed: feminine — where nothing visibly changes
neuter — where nothing changes either
the same noun as a subject, so der comes back

mistake.why: The object takes den: Ich sehe den Apfel.

sentences.usage: Saying what you can see, which is where the accusative first shows.
sentences.mnemonic: Only the masculine shows its accusative.

words.note: The au is the same sound as in Auto and blau. Of hair and eyes German says braun where English also says brown.

sentences.trap: The object is first and the subject is third, and the sentence still means what S03 meant. den is what makes that possible — English would have to say "the apple eats me" and mean it.
sentences.sound: dayn AP-fel ES-suh ikh. The stress lands on Apfel, which is what puts it first.

variations.changed: the ordinary order — same meaning
a different object first
a neuter object, where the article does not change

mistake.why: The object takes den wherever it stands: Den Apfel esse ich.

sentences.usage: Putting the important thing first, which German does far more freely than English.
sentences.mnemonic: The article says who does what. Position is free.

sentences.display: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch
sentences.cue: I'm giving the man the book
sentences.literal: I give to-the man the book

words.note: M1 opened the infinitive geben and the imperative gib. This is the ich cell, and the third person gibt changes its vowel as they do.
The indefinite dative, matching dem. einem Mann, einem Kind — the ending mirrors the definite article throughout.
The feminine dative, matching der. einer Frau — and that is the cell that makes der ambiguous on the page.

sentences.trap: The recipient comes FIRST and the thing second: dem Mann das Buch. Two objects and no preposition between them, and the cases are the only thing keeping them apart.
sentences.sound: ikh GAY-buh daym MAN das BOOKH. dem and den differ by one consonant and by a whole case.

sentences.usage: Handing something over, and the shape every request in M1 was built on.
sentences.mnemonic: Recipient first, thing second, no preposition.

sentences.display: Der Kollegin gebe ich das Buch
sentences.cue: I'm giving the book to the colleague
sentences.literal: To-the colleague give I the book

words.note: die Kollegin is feminine, so its dative article is der — the very three letters that make der Kollege a SUBJECT. The gender of the noun behind the article is what decides which cell you are in.

sentences.trap: der Kollegin is a DATIVE and der Kollege is a nominative. The same three letters, and the gender of the noun behind them is what decides — which is why a noun has to be learnt with its article.
sentences.sound: dair kol-LAY-gin GAY-buh ikh das BOOKH. Kollegin takes its stress on the LAY.

variations.display: Ich gebe der Kollegin das Buch
variations.cue: I'm giving the book to the colleague
variations.changed: the ordinary order — same meaning

variations.display: Dem Mann gebe ich das Buch
variations.cue: I'm giving the man the book
variations.changed: a masculine recipient, where the dative is unmistakable

variations.display: Der Kollege gibt mir das Buch
variations.cue: The colleague is giving me the book
variations.changed: der as a subject — the same word, the other reading

mistake.display: Die Kollegin gebe ich das Buch
mistake.why: The recipient takes the dative: Der Kollegin gebe ich das Buch.

sentences.usage: Putting the recipient first, which German does when they are the point.
sentences.mnemonic: der on a man is a subject. der on a woman is a recipient.

words.note: After ist it takes no ending. The au is the same sound again, and the -er at the end is a light uh.
The -ig ending is said -ich, with the front ch sound, exactly as lustig and ruhig were in M2.

sentences.trap: German negates a noun with kein rather than with nicht. nicht negates a verb or an adjective; kein negates a thing, and it declines exactly like ein.
sentences.sound: das ist kine AP-fel. kein rhymes with English "mine".

variations.changed: feminine, so keine
neuter, which looks like the masculine
an adjective, so nicht rather than kein

mistake.why: A noun is negated with kein: Das ist kein Apfel.

sentences.usage: Correcting someone about what a thing is.
sentences.mnemonic: kein negates a thing, nicht negates everything else.

words.note: Two readings on one word: heavy of a box, difficult of a task. Only the sentence says which, and both are ordinary.
schwer's opposite in both readings at once — light in weight and easy to do. The eicht is said like English "ikes" with a ch on the end.

sentences.trap: nicht goes AFTER the verb and before the adjective. It is not where English puts "not", and its position is one of the things German fixes rather than leaves free.
sentences.sound: dair TISH ist nikht ZOW-ber. The ch of nicht is the front sound.

variations.changed: the positive, with the opposite word
a different quality
the opposite, and it also means easy

mistake.why: nicht follows the verb: Der Tisch ist nicht sauber.

sentences.usage: In a kitchen, a hotel room, or an argument about the washing-up.
sentences.mnemonic: kein for a thing, nicht after the verb.

words.note: Width, where M2 opened length on Haare — breit and its opposite schmal. Both stay predicative here and take no ending after ist.

sentences.trap: Straße keeps its ß. Writing Strasse gives the index a key no row owns, and it is the single most common respelling an English keyboard produces.
sentences.sound: dee SHTRAA-suh ist zair BRITE. The st at the start of a German word is sht, and ei is said eye.

variations.changed: the opposite
M2's length word on a neuter noun
negated

mistake.why: The ß is never respelled: Die Straße ist sehr breit.

sentences.usage: Describing a place, or warning someone about a walk.
sentences.mnemonic: Strasse is a key with no row behind it.

words.note: Masculine — der Löffel — while die Gabel at the same table is feminine. Nothing about either object says so, which is the module's point.
Feminine, and its plural adds -n. Most German nouns ending in -el are masculine, which makes this one worth noticing.

sentences.trap: der Löffel and die Gabel sit next to each other on a table with different genders. A rule that predicted gender from meaning would have to explain that, and none does.
sentences.sound: ine BOOKH ist nikht TOY-er. The eu of teuer is the oy of English "boy".
